finding.mcp-unpinned.detail.other: {names} fetch whatever version is newest each launch, so a bad or hijacked release runs with your tools' access the moment it ships. Pin at least the major version.

finding.mcp-env-secrets.detail.other: {names} receive environment variables, usually API keys, stored in plain text in your Claude config. Know which servers hold which keys, and scope those keys as narrowly as the vendor allows.

finding.perm-none.title: No permission rules set
finding.perm-none.detail: Claude Code is running on its defaults. A short deny list (secrets, force-push, destructive deletes) is the cheapest guardrail there is.
finding.perm-deny-only.title: {count} deny rules, no allow rules
finding.perm-deny-only.detail: You have a safety floor but approve routine commands by hand. Allow-listing the read-only commands you approve every day removes most prompts without widening risk.
finding.agents-none.title: No custom agents defined
finding.agents-none.detail: Agents are saved specialists (a reviewer, a researcher) with their own instructions, tools and model. They keep long tasks out of your main context and let cheap models do cheap work.
finding.agents-model-unset.detail: An agent with no model runs on whatever you are using, often the most expensive one. Naming a lighter model for search and summarising agents cuts spend with no quality loss.
finding.hooks-none.title: No hooks configured
finding.hooks-none.detail: Hooks run your own script on events like session end or before a tool call. They are how a rule becomes automatic instead of something you hope the model remembers.
finding.mix-top-heavy.title: {pct}% of spend is on the largest models
finding.mix-top-heavy.detail: {top} of {known} in 30 days went to the top tier. Searching files, reading logs and summarising do as well a tier down; giving those jobs to subagents on a lighter model is the usual way to cut this without touching the hard work.
finding.areas-unsorted.title: {pct}% of spend has no work area
finding.areas-unsorted.detail: {unsorted} in 30 days came from sessions that started at the top of a workspace and never moved. Starting Claude Code inside the folder you are working on makes the split by area, and by client, exact.
finding.session-long-lived.title: One session has been open {days} days
finding.session-long-lived.detail: It cost {cost} in the last 30 days. A session re-sends its growing history on every turn, so an old one pays more for each answer and gets slower to steer. Starting fresh for new work, and keeping what matters in project memory, is cheaper.

finding.mcp-duplicate-processes.detail: {names} each have several copies live right now; {worstName} alone is running {times} on {mb} MB. Every app you have configured a server in starts its own copy and keeps it for the session, so the same tool is in memory once per client. About {wasted} MB is duplicate. Removing a server from the clients that do not use it, or quitting an app you are not working in, gets it back.

finding.mcp-memory.detail.one: {count} server is live across {processes}, the largest being {topName} at {topMb} MB. They start when a client asks for them and stay for the session, so this is the resting cost of the tools you have wired up rather than anything running away.
finding.mcp-memory.detail.other: {count} servers are live across {processes}, the largest being {topName} at {topMb} MB. They start when a client asks for them and stay for the session, so this is the resting cost of the tools you have wired up rather than anything running away.
finding.pricing-cache-ttl.title: Spend here reads about {pct}% low: 1-hour cache writes
finding.pricing-cache-ttl.detail: Claude Code records what it was actually charged. Over the recent sessions it billed ${totalVendor} where this app's figures come to ${totalOurs} for the same tokens ({names}). The whole difference is the cache writes: they were made with the one-hour cache, which bills at twice the input rate, and this app prices every cache write at the five-minute rate. The logs do not record which cache a write used, so the app cannot tell them apart yet. Token counts are unaffected; read the dollar figures as a floor, not a ceiling.
finding.pricing-drift.title.one: This app's prices disagree with the vendor's on 1 model
finding.pricing-drift.title.other: This app's prices disagree with the vendor's on {count} models
finding.pricing-drift.detail: Claude Code records what it was charged. For the same tokens, this app's rate card says ${ours} where the vendor recorded ${vendor} on {model}: {pct}% {direction}. Affected: {names}. Either the rate card is out of date or the two count tokens differently, so treat every dollar figure here as approximate until it is checked. Everything else in the app measures tokens, which are facts; only the prices are in question.
